charts.title: Planted check: on reports simulated from the reputation model, does the reputation model win?
charts.takeaway: It failed: the reputation model lost to fixed cost by 0.0003 nats per report on its own simulated data, and beat size-of-lie cost by 0.0005.
charts.units: difference in held-out log loss on simulated data, nats per report (a nat is the unit of log loss, the penalty for giving low probability to what happened); above 0 means the reputation model predicts better
charts.n: one simulated data set on the same treatments and the same split by paper
charts.no_interval: The planted check was run once, so the result file holds one difference per rule.
charts.threshold: The reputation model had to beat both the fixed-cost and the size-of-lie models on data simulated from itself
charts.planted: Failed. The pipeline did not recover the reputation model from its own simulated data, so the ranking of theories in the loss chart carries little weight.

charts.title: Reproduction check: mean standardised report in our subset against the published figure.
charts.takeaway: Our subset gives 0.287 against the published 0.234, a difference of 0.053 where the tolerance set in advance was 0.03: the check failed.
charts.units: mean standardised report (0 is what honest reporting gives on average, 1 is everyone reporting the top-paying outcome)
charts.n: 252 treatments in our subset (first rounds only, several designs dropped); the published figure covers the full data
charts.no_interval: The result file holds one mean for the subset. The published figure and the tolerance come from the locked preregistration text.
charts.baseline: Published mean for the full data: 0.234
charts.threshold: Within 0.03 of 0.234; not met. The 0.287 was printed before the lock, so the outcome was knowable when the plan was written.

axis.label: mean standardised report (0 is honest on average)

charts.title: How much better each theory of lying predicts held-out reports than assuming everyone is honest.
charts.takeaway: All six theories gain about 0.07 nats per report and sit within 0.0035 of each other, far above the shuffle control's range; a training average with no theory gains 0.068.
charts.units: gain in held-out log loss over the everyone-honest model, in nats per report (a nat is the unit of log loss, the penalty for giving low probability to what happened); higher is a better prediction
charts.n: 9,960 subjects in 19 held-out papers; models fitted on 17,079 subjects in other papers
charts.interval: Band: 5th to 95th percentile of the best gain after report labels were shuffled within each held-out treatment, 300 draws. Tick: the shuffle mean.
charts.baseline: Everyone honest scores 0 on this axis (loss 1.3202). Shuffle control: mean −0.112, 95th percentile −0.086
charts.threshold: Best gain above the shuffle control's 95th percentile: held, 0.072 against −0.086 (p from draws 0.003)
charts.ruled_out: A difference between the six theories larger than 0.0035 nats per report on these papers. No contrast against the fixed-cost model passes the false-discovery correction (smallest p 0.40).

axis.label: gain over everyone honest, nats per report (higher is better)

charts.title: Edge of the two richer models over the fixed-cost model on held-out papers.
charts.takeaway: Both intervals include zero: reputation is ahead of fixed cost by 0.003 (−0.001 to 0.008) and the full model by 0.002 (−0.008 to 0.012).
charts.units: difference in held-out log loss, nats per report (a nat is the unit of log loss, the penalty for giving low probability to what happened); above 0 means the richer model predicts better than fixed cost
charts.n: 9,960 subjects in 19 held-out papers; models fitted on 17,079 subjects in other papers
charts.interval: 95 percent interval from the result file
charts.baseline: No edge over the fixed-cost model: 0
charts.ruled_out: An edge over fixed cost larger than 0.008 for the reputation model and 0.012 for the full model (upper ends of the intervals)

axis.label: edge over fixed cost, nats per report (above 0 is better)

table: Full minus fixed cost without Effron et al. 2015

charts.title: How people report when a task has three or more outcomes: honest, maximal or partial.
charts.takeaway: Held-out reports read as 45 percent honest, 26 percent maximal (the top-paying outcome) and 29 percent partial (a lie short of the top); the training papers gave 42, 24 and 34.
charts.units: percent of reports, read from the report distribution of each treatment with 3, 6 or 10 outcomes
charts.n: 9,960 subjects in 19 held-out papers; models fitted on 17,079 subjects in other papers
charts.no_interval: The result file holds one share per part with no interval.
charts.baseline: Training papers, and the shares the closest-fitting model predicts for the held-out tasks (Norm, mean absolute error 0.109)
